summary: Gives the profile for DCCP Congestion Control ID 2, which behaves like TCP's congestion control. It suits senders that want to take advantage of available bandwidth in rapidly changing conditions and can cope with the abrupt window changes typical of TCP's additive increase, multiplicative decrease. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A way of sharing the road that speeds up a little at a time and slams on the brakes when it sees a jam, just as TCP does.

questions: how does dccp tcp-like congestion control work
what is ack ratio in dccp
subtitle: How DCCP can borrow TCP's congestion control, including for its acknowledgements, without ever retransmitting data.

tldr.problem: DCCP senders need a congestion control mechanism that takes as much bandwidth as is available in rapidly changing conditions, and that is well understood.
tldr.mechanism: CCID 2 runs a close variant of SACK-based TCP congestion control in packets rather than bytes, using the Ack Vector to learn what arrived, and it also controls the rate of acknowledgements through an Ack Ratio.
tldr.outcome: Senders get TCP-like dynamics, including abrupt halving of the congestion window, over an unreliable datagram service. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8311.

facts.label: Minimum quiescence time T
facts.value: 0.2 seconds or two RTTs, whichever is greater

today: RFC 4341 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2006 and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 8311. It defines CCID 2 for DCCP, the TCP-like alternative to CCID 3 in RFC 4342.

sections.title: What CCID 2 Is
sections.content:
This RFC is the profile for Congestion Control Identifier 2 (CCID 2), called TCP-like Congestion Control, in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340). DCCP uses CCIDs to choose the congestion control mechanism in use on a half-connection, which is the application data sent by one endpoint plus the acknowledgements sent back by the other.

CCID 2 sends data using a close variant of TCP's congestion control, with a variant of selective acknowledgements (SACK). It suits senders who can cope with the abrupt changes in the congestion window typical of TCP's Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) behaviour, and particularly senders who want to use the available bandwidth in rapidly changing conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: DCCP lets programs pick a rulebook for not clogging the network. Rulebook number 2 copies the way TCP drives: speed up slowly, slow down fast when there is trouble.

sections.title: When to Use It and How It Differs from TCP
sections.content:
CCID 2 is appropriate for flows that want as much bandwidth as possible over the long term and can tolerate large sending rate swings, including halving of the congestion window after a congestion event. Applications that simply need to move as much data as possible in as short a time as possible should use it. This contrasts with CCID 3 (TFRC, RFC 4342), which suits flows that prefer to avoid abrupt rate changes.

The RFC recommends CCID 2 over CCID 3 for streaming media that buffers a good deal of data at the receiver before playback, and for applications where halving the rate is unlikely to hurt performance. It also notes that TCP-like dynamics are reasonably well understood.

The mechanisms follow those standardized for SACK-based TCP, but there are three differences. CCID 2 applies congestion control to acknowledgements, which TCP does not. Parameters such as cwnd are counted in packets, not bytes. And because DCCP never retransmits, mechanisms that tell retransmissions from new packets were redesigned. Implementations SHOULD wait for explicit updates to CCID 2 rather than track TCP's evolution directly.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to move lots of stuff fast and do not mind slowing down suddenly, this is your rulebook. It is like TCP, except nothing lost is ever sent again, and even the thank-you notes follow traffic rules.

sections.title: Setting Up a CCID 2 Half-Connection
sections.content:
Use of the Ack Vector is MANDATORY on CCID 2 half-connections. The sender therefore MUST send a Change R(Send Ack Vector, 1) option to the receiver as part of connection establishment.

The sender SHOULD NOT send data until it has received the matching Confirm L(Send Ack Vector, 1), except that it MAY send data on DCCP-Request packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the sender starts, it asks the receiver to promise to report exactly which packets arrived. It waits for the promise before sending much.

sections.title: Congestion Control on Data Packets
sections.content:
The sender keeps three integer values, all measured in packets: the congestion window cwnd (the maximum number of data packets allowed in the network), the slow-start threshold ssthresh, and pipe, its estimate of how many data packets are outstanding. The sender MAY send a data packet when pipe < cwnd and MUST NOT when pipe >= cwnd. Each data packet sent adds 1 to pipe.

The sender lowers pipe by 1 for each data packet newly acknowledged as received, and for each packet inferred lost. A packet is inferred lost when at least NUMDUPACK packets sent after it have been acknowledged as received; NUMDUPACK is three, as in TCP. After a transmit timeout, handled like TCP's retransmission timeout, the sender sets pipe to zero. Because DCCP does not retransmit data, it does not need TCP's recommended minimum timeout of one second.

On each congestion event (at least one lost or marked packet), cwnd is halved and ssthresh is set to the new cwnd, with cwnd never below one packet. After a timeout, ssthresh becomes cwnd/2 and cwnd becomes one packet. In slow start (cwnd < ssthresh) the window grows by one packet for every two newly acknowledged unmarked data packets, up to Ack Ratio/2 packets per acknowledgement. Above the threshold it grows by one packet per window of data acknowledged without loss or marks. The initial cwnd is at most four packets.

The RFC also covers receiver feedback. A Drop Code 2 (receive buffer drop) reduces cwnd by one per packet, never below one, and the sender MUST exit slow start on a relevant Data Dropped or Slow Receiver option. CCID 2 is optimized for applications with a fixed packet size that vary packets per second; it is not appropriate for applications that fix the interval between packets and vary packet size instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender counts how many packets are out on the road and only sends more when there is room. When it spots a loss it cuts its allowance in half, and then slowly grows it back.

sections.title: Acknowledgements and Ack Ratio
sections.content:
Each required acknowledgement MUST carry Ack Vector options that say exactly which packets arrived and whether they were ECN-marked. The sender uses DCCP's Ack Ratio feature to influence how often the receiver sends a DCCP-Ack, which controls congestion on the reverse path. The default Ack Ratio is two, and with it CCID 2 behaves like TCP with delayed acks.

All receiver packets carry sequence numbers, so the sender can detect lost or marked acknowledgements. Ack Ratio depends on losses and marks of non-data packets only. Unless it has better information, the sender SHOULD assume every lost receiver packet was a non-data packet; DCCP's NDP Count option can tell it more.

For every window of data containing a lost or marked DCCP-Ack, the sender doubles Ack Ratio, halving the acknowledgement rate. For each cwnd/(R2 minus R) consecutive congestion windows with no such loss or mark, where R is the current Ack Ratio, it decreases Ack Ratio by 1. Ack Ratio stays an integer, and the sender SHOULD NOT renegotiate it more than once per round-trip time.

An active sender MUST also occasionally acknowledge the receiver's acknowledgements so the receiver can free its Ack Vector state, and SHOULD do so at least once per congestion window. A receiver decides the sender is quiescent after T seconds without data, where T is the greater of 0.2 seconds and two round-trip times, and after the sender has acknowledged all its Ack Vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender also tells the receiver how often to send thank-you notes. If the notes themselves get lost in traffic, the sender asks for half as many, and then slowly asks for more again.

sections.title: ECN and Related Options
sections.content:
CCID 2 supports Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN, RFC 3168). The sender uses the ECN Nonce on data packets, and the receiver echoes the nonces in its Ack Vectors, so the sender SHOULD check them against expected values to catch accidental or malicious concealment of marks. Because Ack Vector information is reliably delivered, DCCP does not need the TCP flags ECN-Echo and Congestion Window Reduced.

Acknowledgements are congestion controlled, so ECN may be used on them too, but without the nonce. Section 8 lists the DCCP pieces relevant to CCID 2: the Ack Vector option, and the ECN Capable, Ack Ratio and Send Ack Vector features.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can wave a flag that says the road is getting busy instead of dropping packets. The receiver reports those flags back, and a secret number makes it hard to hide any of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of DCCP (RFC 4340) and TCP congestion control (RFC 2581). The latter discusses how an attacker could hurt a connection by dropping packets, or by forging extra duplicate acknowledgements or acknowledgements for new data.

The authors are not aware of any new security considerations created by TCP-like congestion control in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys could mess with the road signs, but this rulebook does not add any new ways to do that.
